title: AI Advisory Offer Language
summary: Exact language for selling the AI advisory product, plus CPA-specific email angles.
content:
AI Advisory Offer Language + CPA Email Angles

Date: 2026-03-11 Agent: Alex (Deal Architect) Purpose: Exact language for selling the AI advisory product, plus 5 CPA-specific email angles for Jacob.

Part 1: The Offer Language

The Two-Sentence Pitch ("Geek Squad for AI")

Version A (for CPAs and professional services): "We're the Geek Squad for AI. Small businesses know they need it but have no idea where to start, so we show up, figure out what's eating their time, and build them a system that actually runs."

Version B (for contractors directly): "Think of us as the Geek Squad for AI, but for your business operations. We come in, find the 5 things burning your hours every week, and automate them so you can focus on the work that makes money."

Version C (shortest, for casual conversation): "We're like Geek Squad but for AI. We set it up, we keep it running, you don't have to think about it."

What the Audit Actually Covers (Concrete, Not Vague)

The $2,500 AI Operations Audit includes:

  1. Tool inventory. What software are you paying for? What are you actually using? Most businesses are paying for 3-4 tools they barely touch and missing 2-3 that would save them hours.

  2. Time drain mapping. Where does your week go? We sit with you (or your office manager) and map every recurring task: scheduling, invoicing, follow-ups, estimates, material ordering, customer communication. We find the ones that are repetitive, predictable, and eating your day.

  3. Communication audit. How does information move through your team? Phone calls, texts, emails, sticky notes, verbal? We map the gaps where things fall through the cracks, jobs get double-booked, or customers wait too long for a callback.

  4. AI opportunity scoring. Every time drain gets scored on two axes: how much time it wastes (impact) and how easy it is to automate (feasibility). You get a ranked list, not a vague "you should use AI more."

  5. The Roadmap. A deliverable you keep. Top 5-7 automation opportunities ranked by ROI. Each one includes: what it does, how much time it saves per week, what it costs to build, and a timeline. This isn't a pitch deck. It's a blueprint.

Timeline: 1 week from kickoff to deliverable. Format: 2-3 hour discovery session (on-site preferred, video works) + 1 week analysis + roadmap delivery meeting.

The Pricing Conversation Flow

Step 1: Lead with the audit. "We start with a $2,500 audit. We come in, look at how your business actually runs day to day, and come back with a roadmap of what AI can realistically do for you. Specific automations, specific time savings, specific costs. Not theory. If you look at the roadmap and decide it's not worth pursuing, you still have a document you can use with anyone."

Step 2: Let the roadmap sell the build. "Most clients look at the roadmap and pick the top 2-3 items to build first. That's typically a $5,000-$8,000 project depending on complexity. We build it, train your team on it, and support it for 30 days after launch."

Step 3: The retainer introduces itself. "AI moves fast. Systems need tuning. New automations come up as your business changes. Most clients move to a monthly retainer, $1,500-$3,000/month, where we keep everything running, optimize what's built, and add new automations as needs come up. Think of it like having an AI department without hiring one."

What NOT to say:

  • Don't lead with "multi-agent system" or "agentic AI." Nobody cares about the architecture.
  • Don't compare to enterprise tools. It scares people on price.
  • Don't promise specific hour savings before the audit. The audit is where the numbers come from.
  • Don't say "AI strategy." Say "we figure out what's eating your time and fix it."

What Makes AOM Different

vs. Deloitte / McKinsey / Big Consulting: "They charge $50k minimum and send you a deck. We charge $2,500, show up at your office, and build the thing. We work with businesses that have 5-50 employees, not 5,000."

vs. Generic AI Consultants: "Most AI consultants sell advice. We sell systems. We don't hand you a report and wish you luck. We build the automation, train your team, and manage it month to month. And because we also do your video, website, and social media, you're not managing 4 vendors. You're managing one."

vs. DIY (ChatGPT, Zapier, Make): "ChatGPT is a tool. We build a system. Using ChatGPT for your business is like having a brilliant employee who forgets everything every morning. We build the employee, give them a brain, a process, and make it permanent. Most business owners try ChatGPT for two weeks and stop because they don't know what to ask. We already figured that out."

vs. Estes Media / Construction AI competitors: "They sell marketing tools that happen to use AI. We build operational systems. Scheduling, estimating, invoicing, customer communication, internal knowledge. The stuff that actually runs your business, not just your ads."

The real differentiator (use in conversations, not in emails): "We run our own business on a multi-agent AI system. 12 AI agents handle our outreach, our design, our QA, our strategy, our scheduling. We didn't read about this in a book. We built it, we use it every day, and we're building the same thing for our clients. Nobody else in Phoenix can say that."

Industry-Specific Pain Points to Reference

For CPAs:

  • Manual data entry from client documents
  • Chasing clients for missing paperwork
  • Repetitive email responses during tax season
  • Staff burnout from seasonal volume spikes
  • Client onboarding that takes too long

For Contractors (when talking to CPAs about their clients):

  • Scheduling crews across multiple jobs
  • Estimating that takes hours instead of minutes
  • Customer follow-ups that fall through the cracks
  • Invoice processing and payment tracking
  • Material ordering and inventory
  • Job site documentation and photo management

Part 2: 5 CPA Email Angles for Jacob

Context for Jacob: These are NOT cold pitches for AOM's AI advisory service directly. These follow Jacob's existing approach: partnership/referral plays first, AI mentioned casually in 1 out of 5. The difference from Batch 1 is that these angles are specifically designed to introduce the AI advisory concept through the CPA relationship, not sell it head-on.

Rules (same as Batch 1):

  • Patrik's voice. Real, casual, specific.
  • Each email references a real detail about the person/firm.
  • AI mention: max 1 out of 5 emails.
  • "After tax season" / "after April 15" timing baked in.
  • No case studies in cold emails. No positioning language.

ANGLE 1: Tax Season Overwhelm

Use when: The CPA is a small firm (1-5 people) that clearly gets crushed during tax season. Solo practitioners are ideal.

Subject line: "quick thought after seeing [Firm Name]"

Opening hook: Acknowledge the brutality of tax season directly. Don't pretend you know what it's like. Just observe that they're in the trenches.

Value prop: AOM works with small businesses that need operational help. The angle: "Your clients come to you stressed about their business. When the stress is about visibility, marketing, or getting more work, that's our lane. You'd have someone to point them to instead of just saying 'yeah, you should do social media.'"

CTA: "After April 15, would a 15-minute call make sense? I know right now is survival mode."

Example draft:

[Name], I know you're deep in it right now and the last thing you need is another email. I'll keep this short.

I run a production company in Phoenix that helps small businesses with their video and web presence, mostly in the trades. I've been looking for CPAs who work with the same types of business owners I do. Seems like [Firm Name] is one of them.

When tax season ends and your clients start asking about growth, I'd love to be someone you can point them to for the marketing side. We'd send people your way too.

After April 15, worth a quick call?

ANGLE 2: Staff Shortage / Automation

Use when: The CPA firm is mid-size (5-15 people) and likely struggling to hire or retain staff. Accounting has a well-documented talent shortage.

Subject line: "really impressed by [Firm Name] work"

Opening hook: Reference something specific about the firm (years in business, specialization, community involvement). Then pivot to the connection.

Value prop: "We work with small businesses that are trying to do more with fewer people. That sounds like everyone right now, but it's especially true in the trades. When one of your clients is growing but can't find staff to keep up, the first thing that usually falls off is their marketing and online presence. That's where we come in."

CTA: "Would it make sense to connect sometime after your busy season?"

Example draft:

[Name], I came across [Firm Name] and noticed [specific detail: years in business, specialty, community work]. That kind of [longevity/focus/commitment] stood out.

I run a creative production company in Phoenix. We help small businesses, mostly contractors and trades, stay visible even when they're stretched thin on staff. A lot of the business owners I talk to are trying to do more with fewer people, and I imagine your clients are saying the same thing.

If a client ever mentions needing help getting their work in front of more people, I'd be happy to be that referral. Goes both ways.

Open to connecting after tax season?

ANGLE 3: Client Retention Through AI Services (AI MENTION EMAIL)

Use when: The CPA positions themselves as a "strategic advisor" or "business advisor," not just a tax preparer. They talk about helping clients grow, not just file. This is the 1-in-5 AI mention email.

Subject line: "interesting overlap between [Firm Name] and what I'm building"

Opening hook: Reference their advisory positioning. "You're clearly more than a tax shop."

Value prop: "We do creative production (video, web, social) for small businesses. Lately I've also been building AI operations systems for business owners, things like automated scheduling, inbox management, and workflow automation. Not sure if that's useful for your clients, but it's been an interesting build."

The AI mention is casual and uncertain. "Not sure if that's useful" is intentional. It invites curiosity without pitching.

CTA: "Either way, sounds like we work with similar people. Worth a conversation sometime?"

Example draft:

[Name], I looked into [Firm Name] and it's clear you're doing more than tax prep. [Specific detail: advisory services, business consulting, growth focus]. That's a rare CPA.

I run a production company in Phoenix. We do video, websites, and social for small businesses. Recently I've also been building AI systems for business owners to help with things like scheduling automation, inbox triage, and keeping the back office running without hiring more people. I'm not sure how relevant that is for your clients, but it's been pretty interesting to build.

Either way, seems like we're working with the same type of person. Would a conversation make sense after April?

ANGLE 4: Competitive Advantage

Use when: The CPA serves a niche (construction, medical, restaurants, tech). They've deliberately specialized, which means they understand differentiation.

Subject line: "really impressed by [Firm Name] [niche] focus"

Opening hook: Acknowledge their specialization. "Most CPAs try to serve everyone. You picked [niche] and went all in. That tells me something."

Value prop: "I work with [same niche or adjacent] businesses on their marketing. Your clients already have an edge because they're working with a CPA who actually understands their industry. If they also had a marketing partner who gets their world, they'd be hard to compete with."

CTA: "I'd love to compare notes on what we're both seeing in [niche]. Quick call after April 15?"

Example draft:

[Name], I noticed [Firm Name] focuses specifically on [niche]. Most firms try to be everything to everyone. The fact that you picked a lane tells me you understand your clients at a level most CPAs don't.

I run AOM, a production company in Phoenix. We do video, websites, and social media for [same/adjacent niche] businesses. I feel like we see the same problems from different angles. If any of your [niche] clients want to stand out from their competitors online, I'd be a natural referral. We'd return the favor.

Would a quick call work after tax season?

ANGLE 5: Cost Savings / Efficiency

Use when: The CPA emphasizes cost management, profitability analysis, or operational efficiency for clients. They're already thinking about the bottom line.

Subject line: "thought of [Firm Name] when looking at this"

Opening hook: "You help your clients save money. I help them make more of it."

Value prop: "When a business gets their marketing right, they stop relying on word of mouth alone and start controlling their pipeline. That's a profitability conversation, not a marketing conversation. And I imagine you've had clients who are great at their work but invisible online. That invisibility costs them jobs."

CTA: "Worth a 15-minute call to see if there's a referral fit?"

Example draft:

[Name], I was looking at [Firm Name] and noticed your focus on [profitability/efficiency/cost management] for your clients. That's the part of accounting I find most interesting, honestly.

I run a production company in Phoenix that helps small businesses get visible. Video, websites, social media, mostly for contractors and trades. Here's the overlap I see: you're helping your clients keep more of what they earn. We're helping them earn more by making them findable. Both sides of the same coin.

If a client ever mentions wanting more work or better leads, I'd be an easy recommendation. Happy to send business your way too.

Worth a quick call after the rush?

Part 3: How Jacob Should Use These

Selection Logic

Pick the angle based on what you find during research on each CPA:

If you find this... Use this angle
Solo practitioner, clearly swamped Angle 1 (Tax Season Overwhelm)
Mid-size firm, hiring posts, "growing team" language Angle 2 (Staff Shortage)
"Strategic advisor" positioning, advisory services listed Angle 3 (Client Retention / AI Mention)
Niche specialization (construction, medical, restaurant) Angle 4 (Competitive Advantage)
Efficiency/profitability language on their site Angle 5 (Cost Savings)

AI Mention Frequency

  • 1 out of every 5 emails gets the AI mention (Angle 3).
  • The other 4 are pure partnership/referral plays.
  • The AI mention is always casual, always uncertain ("not sure if that's useful"), never a pitch.
  • Let them ask. Curiosity converts better than pressure.

Personalization Rules (Same as Batch 1)

  • Every email must have a specific, real detail about the person. Swap the name and the email should break.
  • No templates that work with a find-and-replace.
  • Varied language. No two emails should open the same way.
  • "After tax season" or "after April 15" in every email. Respect their reality.

What to Track

For every CPA email sent, log in cold-outreach-log.md:

  • [CPA] tag (separate from [CONTRACTOR] and [PARTNER])
  • Which angle was used (1-5)
  • Whether AI was mentioned (yes/no)
  • Reply tracking: who replies, what they say, which angle worked

This data tells Alex which positioning resonates. After 20-30 CPA emails, we'll know which angle to double down on.

Part 4: Pricing Objection Handlers

"$2,500 for an audit? I can use ChatGPT for free." "You can. Most people do for about two weeks. The audit isn't about AI tools. It's about understanding how your business actually operates and finding where you're losing time. ChatGPT doesn't sit in your office and watch how your team works."

"We're too small for AI." "That's actually the sweet spot. Big companies have IT departments that handle this. Small businesses have you and maybe an office manager. The audit finds the 3-4 things that eat your week and shows you how to automate them. The smaller you are, the more each hour matters."

"I don't trust AI." "That's fair. Neither did most of our clients until they saw what it does with something specific. We don't replace people. We handle the repetitive stuff so your people can do the work that actually requires their brain."

"What's the ROI?" "That's exactly what the audit answers. We don't guess. We measure your actual time drains, score them, and show you the math. If the numbers don't make sense, we'll tell you."

"I already use [ServiceTitan / Buildertrend / Housecall Pro]." "Good. Those are solid tools. The audit often finds that businesses are using 40% of what those tools can do. We help you use the other 60%, and we connect them to each other so data doesn't live in silos."
